newsitem.title: GERMANY: German union threatens strike, says law on its side.
newsitem.headline: German union threatens strike, says law on its side.

text.p: Germany's IG Metall union on Monday repeated warnings that it was prepared to strike over planned cuts to workers' sick pay and said such cuts would in most cases represent a breach of contract.

"If required IG Metall will not shy away from a strike to maintain sick payments (at the full 100 percent level)," Klaus Zwickel, chairman of the metal and electronics sector union IG Metall, told a news briefing.
Zwickel was referring to a recently-passed government law aimed at reducing sick pay to 80 percent of workers' salaries.

He said the union had sought legal opinion that had concluded that "well over 80 percent", or some three million workers in the sector, had contracts with "autonomous and independent" clauses protecting sick payments at 100 percent.
Zwickel raised the spectre of the 114-day strike 40 years ago in Schleswig-Holstein with which unions secured the sick pay agreements in the first place.
"At the end of this conflict, this republic will not slip back to the state of affairs in 1956," Zwickel said.
He noted that a country-wide day of protest being organised by IG Metall was to be held on October 24 -- that day on which the Schleswig-Holstein strike began.
